content.title: About
content.content: Chinese cabbage (Brassica rapa subsp. pekinensis) is a leafy vegetable widely used in Asian cuisine. When cooked with a small amount of fat, the leaves become tender, aromatic, and retain a slight crunch. The dish is rich in B‑vitamins, vitamin C, minerals, and contains a modest amount of fat from cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chinese cabbage is a staple in stir‑fries and soups across China.
In Chinese it is called “bao cai” and is considered a symbol of longevity.
Cooking it with a little oil helps preserve nutrients better than long boiling in water.
Leaves can be used as wrappers for rolls and steamed dishes.
Traditional Chinese medicine classifies it as a cooling food that helps reduce internal “heat.”

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is important for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps you feel full.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phytonutrients in cabbage help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Low sodium and potassium content help maintain normal blood pressure.

items.title: Cruciferous vegetable allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cabbage.

items.title: Glucosinolates content
items.content: Excessive intake of glucosinolates may affect thyroid function.

items.title: Added fat
items.content: The dish contains added fat, so people watching calorie intake should control portion size.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the cabbage as a side dish, add it to soups, stews, or stir‑fry with other vegetables. Cook with a small amount of oil (such as sunflower or sesame) to retain flavor and texture. Serve hot, garnished with fresh ginger or scallions.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh cabbage in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, wrapped in a perforated bag. Cooked portions should be stored in an airtight container for up to 3‑4 days. Discard if any off‑odors or signs of spoilage appear.

content.title: About
content.content: Date is the sweet fruit of the date palm (Phoenix dactylifera), native to the arid regions of the Middle East, North Africa, and South Asia. The fruits are dark brown, soft‑fleshed, and have a characteristic caramel‑like sweetness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The date palm can reach up to 30 m in height and live for more than 150 years.
Dates have been cultivated for over 6 000 years, making them one of the oldest cultivated crops.
There are more than 200 varieties of dates, differing in size, color, and sweetness level.
Dates are often called a “natural energy bar” because of their high natural sugar content.
In ancient cultures dates were used in rituals and offered as gifts to deities.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Dates provide both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and blood‑sugar regulation.

items.title: High in potassium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain fluid balance, blood pressure, and proper muscle function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids, carotenoids, and phenolic compounds protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Heart‑friendly nutrients
items.content: Monounsaturated fats and magnesium contribute to lower LDL cholesterol levels.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: Vitamins B6, B5, and folate are involved in energy metabolism and red blood‑cell formation.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Because dates are rich in natural sugars, they can raise the glycemic index and should be limited by people with diabetes.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Dates are calorie‑dense; excessive consumption may lead to weight gain.

items.title: Allergy potential
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to dates.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: High oxalate levels may contribute to kidney‑stone formation in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dates can be eaten as a snack, added to cereals, yogurt, smoothies, baked goods, or used as a natural sweetener. They are often stuffed with nuts, cheese, or chocolate.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dates in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For long‑term storage, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer, where they stay fresh for up to a year.

pasta-with-cream-sauce-and-added-vegetab.title: Pasta with Cream Sauce and Added Vegetables, Ready‑to‑Heat

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with cream sauce and added vegetables is a ready‑to‑heat meal that can be quickly warmed in a microwave or on the stove. It contains durum wheat pasta, a creamy sauce made from dairy ingredients, and a mix of vegetables (carrot, broccoli, red pepper). The dish is balanced in protein, carbohydrates and fats, making it suitable for a fast lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cream sauce is prepared with cream, butter and a small amount of flour, giving the dish a silky texture.
Vegetables are blanched before being mixed in to retain bright colour and a slight crunch.
Ready‑to‑heat pasta is often fortified with B‑vitamins and iron to boost its nutritional profile.
The product is packaged in single‑serve containers, popular among busy consumers.
It should be heated to at least 75 °C to ensure thorough warming without drying out.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Pasta provides sustained energy and a feeling of fullness thanks to its slow‑release glucose.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: The included vegetables (broccoli, carrot, red pepper) supply vitamin C, vitamin A and folate.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D from the cream
items.content: The creamy sauce contributes calcium for bone health and vitamin D when fortified.

items.title: Dietary fiber content
items.content: Vegetables add fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Protein from plant and dairy sources
items.content: Combined wheat and dairy proteins aid muscle maintenance.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The cream sauce contains lactose, so those with intolerance should choose a lactose‑free version.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: The creamy sauce increases the calorie density; portion control is advised for weight‑watchers.

items.title: Wheat allergy / gluten sensitivity
items.content: Durum wheat pasta may trigger reactions in individuals with gluten‑related disorders.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Salt is added for flavor; people with hypertension should monitor total sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the meal in the microwave (2–3 minutes) or on the stovetop, stirring until hot. Serve immediately; optional toppings include fresh basil, grated Parmesan, or a pinch of black pepper.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0–4 °C for up to 5 days. After opening, seal tightly with a lid or film. When frozen, the product remains good for up to 2 months; thaw in the refrigerator before reheating.

content.title: About
content.content: Ready‑to‑Eat Popcorn (NFS) is an airy, lightly salted and flavored corn snack prepared by dry‑popping. It retains the natural corn taste, has a crisp texture, and is convenient for a quick bite.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Popcorn is one of the few grains that “pops” when heated, creating a light, airy structure.
The first commercial popcorn appeared in the United States in the late 19th century.
Popcorn is a staple in movie theaters: over 3 billion servings are sold each year.
There are more than 30 flavor variants, from classic salted to caramel, cheese, and spicy chili.
Popcorn without added oil or sugar is considered a low‑calorie snack.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Air‑popped popcorn without oil contains about 350 kcal per 100 g, making it a lighter alternative to many fried snacks.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber in popcorn supports digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Polysaccharides and polyphenols in corn have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Popcorn is naturally gluten‑free, safe for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Popcorn provides thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Excessively salty popcorn can contribute to high blood pressure.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may have an allergic reaction to corn.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Small popcorn pieces can pose a choking risk for young children.

items.title: Additives and flavorings
items.content: Some varieties contain artificial flavorings and preservatives that may cause sensitivities.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Ready‑to‑Eat popcorn can be consumed straight from the bag. It works as a standalone snack, can be added to salads, used in recipes, or mixed with dried fruit and nuts for a trail‑mix.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store popcorn in a sealed package in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep it in the refrigerator to maintain crunch and prevent moisture absorption.

pork-rice-and-vegetables-including-carro.title: Pork, Rice, and Vegetables with Tomato Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of lean pork, boiled rice and vegetables (carrot, broccoli, dark‑green leafy greens) in a flavorful tomato‑based sauce. Pork provides high‑quality protein, rice supplies complex carbohydrates, and the vegetables add vitamins, minerals and fiber. The sauce, made from ripe tomatoes, onion and spices, gives the meal a rich taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pork is one of the most widely consumed meats worldwide.
Rice has been a staple energy source in Asian cuisine for over 5,000 years.
Broccoli contains more vitamin C than an orange.
Tomatoes were first domesticated in South America more than 7,000 years ago.
Combining protein, carbs and vegetables makes the dish nutritionally balanced.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Pork supplies all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin A and beta‑carotene
items.content: Carrots and tomato sauce are high in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.

items.title: Supports immune function
items.content: Broccoli and leafy greens provide vitamin C, folate and antioxidants that boost immunity.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetables and whole‑grain rice add fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Provides sustained energy
items.content: Complex carbs from rice release glucose slowly, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Fatty cuts of pork can raise cholesterol if eaten in excess.

items.title: Added salt in sauce
items.content: Tomato sauces often contain added salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes or spices.

items.title: Foodborne pathogens
items.content: Undercooked pork may harbor bacteria such as Salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, mixing pork pieces, rice and vegetables in the sauce. Garnish with fresh herbs, a squeeze of lemon, or a pinch of chili for extra flavor. It works well as a main course for lunch or dinner.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool leftovers to room temperature, then place in an airtight container and refrigerate for up to 3 days. Reheat thoroughly before eating to eliminate any possible bacteria.

shrimp-and-vegetables-in-sauce-with-nood.title: Shrimp and Vegetables in Sauce with Noodles (Diet Frozen Meal)

content.title: About
content.content: Shrimp and vegetables in sauce with noodles is a ready‑to‑heat frozen meal designed for diet‑friendly nutrition. It contains peeled shrimp, a mix of fresh vegetables (bell pepper, carrot, broccoli), a light tomato‑cream sauce, and whole‑grain noodles. The dish cooks quickly in a microwave or on the stovetop while retaining flavor and texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shrimp are a high‑quality source of protein with very little fat, making them popular in weight‑loss diets.
The vegetables are steam‑cooked to preserve maximum vitamins and minerals.
The sauce contains only a modest amount of added sugar and salt to meet diet standards.
Whole‑grain noodles provide slower‑release carbohydrates compared with refined pasta.
The product has passed rigorous microbiological testing and meets frozen‑food safety regulations.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Shrimp deliver about 20 g of protein per serving, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: With less than 5 g of fat per portion, most of which are healthy polyunsaturated fats.

items.title: Rich in vitamins and minerals
items.content: Vegetables add vitamin C, vitamin A, potassium and folate, while shrimp provide zinc, selenium and vitamin B12.

items.title: Supports weight control
items.content: At roughly 250 kcal per serving, the meal is low‑calorie yet satiating.

items.title: Heart‑healthy benefits
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids in shrimp help improve lipid profiles.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Shrimp can trigger severe allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Although reduced, the meal still contains about 300 mg of sodium, which should be considered for hypertension.

items.title: Proper heating required
items.content: Insufficient heating may leave live bacteria; heat to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: Contains glutamate
items.content: The sauce may include monosodium glutamate, which some people prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the frozen portion in the microwave (≈3‑4 min) or on the stovetop, stirring to coat the noodles and vegetables evenly with sauce. Serve hot, optionally garnished with fresh herbs or a squeeze of lemon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the product frozen at –18 °C or lower. Once thawed, consume within 24 hours and do not refreeze. Discard if you notice off‑odors or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Chamomile tea is an infusion of dried chamomile flowers (Matricaria chamomilla), usually served hot. It has a mild, slightly sweet flavor and an apple‑like aroma. The drink is popular as a calming beverage, especially in the evening.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chamomile has been used in traditional medicine for over 4,000 years.
Several species exist; the most common is German chamomile (Matricaria recutita).
Ancient Egyptians used chamomile to dye fabrics.
Chamomile tea is often offered in hotels and restaurants as a non‑alcoholic alternative.
Its scent is believed to help improve sleep quality.

items.title: Calms the nervous system
items.content: Flavonoids such as apigenin in chamomile promote relaxation and may reduce anxiety.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: A warm infusion stimulates bile production and can ease stomach cramps.

items.title: Anti‑inflammatory effect
items.content: Antioxidants in chamomile help lower inflammation throughout the body.

items.title: Soothes cold symptoms
items.content: Heat and aroma can relieve nasal congestion and cough.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Asteraceae allergy
items.content: People allergic to plants of the Asteraceae family (e.g., daisies) may react to chamomile.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Chamomile can enhance the effects of sedatives and anticoagulants.

items.title: Pregnancy
items.content: Large amounts of chamomile tea are not recommended for pregnant women without medical advice.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Place 1‑2 teaspoons of dried flowers into 200 ml of boiling water, steep for 5‑10 minutes, then strain. Drink hot, optionally sweetened with honey or a slice of lemon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried flowers in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Shelf life is typically 1‑2 years. Discard if you notice mold odor or loss of aroma.
